opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. When most people started building with LLMs, the natural instinct was to take the way a human would solve a problem, break it into steps, and hard-code that as a workflow: call the model here, retrieve some documents there, check the output, route to the next step. That's a reasonable place to start, and for a lot of narrow, well-defined tasks it still works well.

But I think there are a few fundamental limitations.

The first is that the workflow is only as good as the designer's understanding of the problem. When you write the steps down, you're baking in your assumptions about what the task looks like. Real-world tasks are messy. The moment a user asks something slightly off-distribution, or the data looks different than you expected, the rigid pipeline has no way to adapt. It just follows the script, even when the script no longer makes sense.

The second is that these workflows tend to be brittle in a compounding way. Every step is a place where errors can creep in, and because the steps are chained, a small mistake early on cascades. A human doing the task would notice something's off and backtrack. A fixed workflow usually can't do that unless you've explicitly anticipated that failure mode and built a branch for it, and you end up with this ever-growing tangle of special cases.

The third, which I think is the most important, is that human-designed workflows put a ceiling on what the model can do. The models keep getting more capable at reasoning, planning, and recovering from their own mistakes. If you constrain them to a sequence of steps you designed, you're not letting them use those capabilities. It's a bit like hiring a really smart person and handing them a checklist they're not allowed to deviate from. You get predictability, but you lose most of the value.

What we've seen is that when you instead give the model good tools, a clear objective, and a way to get feedback, and then train or tune it end to end on the actual task, it often finds strategies a person wouldn't have written down, and it handles the long tail of weird cases much more gracefully. That's the shift I'm excited about: moving from designing the workflow to designing the environment, the tools, and the evaluation, and letting the model learn the workflow itself.

That said, I don't think workflows go away entirely. If you need tight guarantees, low latency, or you're in a regulated setting, a well-designed pipeline is often the right call. But for open-ended, complex tasks, I think the field is going to move more and more toward agents that learn how to approach the problem rather than following a script we wrote for them.

r001.rationale: The response says errors can arise at every step and that an early mistake cascades through the chained workflow.

r002.rationale: It describes rigid workflows that bake in assumptions and fail on messy tasks, but does not clearly say they oversimplify the process a real expert would follow.

r003.rationale: It says end-to-end training can lead models to find strategies a person would not have written down, but does not state that rewarding successful task completion teaches workflows better than humans can readily design.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way most people build agents today is they sit down and they think really hard about the problem, and they decompose it into a sequence of steps. First the model does this, then it calls this tool, then it checks the output, then it goes to the next node in the graph. And that works, right? You can get something that functions that way. But I think there are a couple of fundamental problems with it.

The first is that you're basically encoding your own understanding of how to solve the task into the system. And your understanding is limited. The space of situations the agent is going to encounter in the real world is a lot bigger than the space of situations you thought about when you were drawing boxes on a whiteboard. So the moment the agent hits something that's a little bit off-distribution from what you anticipated, the workflow breaks, and it breaks in ways that are kind of brittle and hard to recover from.

The second is that you're putting a ceiling on the system. If I hand-design the workflow, the best the agent can ever do is execute my workflow well. It can't discover a better way of doing the task than the one I came up with. And if you look at the history of machine learning, that's sort of the bitter lesson over and over again: the hand-engineered approach looks good for a while, and then the approach that lets the model learn more of the pipeline end to end wins, because it scales with data and compute in a way that the hand-designed thing doesn't.

And then the third thing, which is maybe the most practical one, is maintenance. Every time the underlying model gets better, your carefully designed workflow is now suboptimal, and in some cases it's actively getting in the way. You built all this scaffolding to compensate for weaknesses in last year's model, and now you have to go rip it out. So teams end up on this treadmill of re-engineering their agents every time there's a new model release.

So I don't think human-designed workflows are useless. They're a really good way to get started, and for narrow, well-understood tasks they're often the right call. But I think the direction things are going is that the models themselves take on more of the responsibility for deciding what to do, and the human's job shifts toward defining what success looks like, giving the agent good tools and good feedback, and evaluating whether it actually got there, rather than specifying step by step how it should get there.

r001.rationale: The response says workflows can break brittly when they encounter situations the designer did not anticipate, but it does not identify errors compounding across steps.

r002.rationale: It says designers encode a limited understanding and impose a ceiling, but does not clearly state that the workflow oversimplifies how a real expert would perform the task.

r003.rationale: It says end-to-end learning can outperform hand-designed workflows, but does not connect that learning to rewards for successful task completion.

astra-6.text:
I think the main limitation is that you’re encoding your own assumptions about how a task should be solved. You’re saying, first retrieve this information, then call this tool, then make this decision. That can work really well when you understand the task and the situations the system is going to encounter. But as the task becomes more open-ended, it gets harder to anticipate all the different paths it might need to take.

And there’s a second issue, which is that the workflow you design might not be the best one. It’s a reasonable starting point, but you’d ideally want the system to learn from experience which steps are useful, when it needs more information, and when it can stop.

The challenge is that giving the model that freedom also makes the system harder to evaluate and debug. So I think there’s an interesting balance: workflows give you structure and predictability, but they can also put a ceiling on how much the system can adapt.

r001.rationale: The response discusses difficulty anticipating paths and adapting, but does not identify errors compounding across workflow steps.

r002.rationale: It says human workflows encode assumptions and may limit adaptation, but does not state that they oversimplify how a real expert would work.

r003.rationale: It mentions learning from experience, but not reward for successful task completion or that models can learn better workflows than humans can readily design.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest limitation is that you’re encoding, up front, your assumptions about how a task should be solved. You’re saying, first retrieve some information, then call this tool, then evaluate the result, and if this particular thing happens, take this branch. That can work really well when you understand the task and the range of situations you’re going to encounter.

But as the task becomes more open-ended, it gets harder to anticipate all those situations. You add another branch for an edge case, and then another, and eventually you have this complicated workflow that’s difficult to maintain. And you may also be constraining the model: it might have enough information to answer already, or it might need to take a step you didn’t anticipate.

So the interesting question is how much of that decision-making we can let the model learn. Can it learn when to use a tool, what information it needs, and when it’s done? There’s a tradeoff, because the explicit workflow gives you control and predictability. But it also puts a ceiling on how much the system can adapt beyond what its designer thought to account for.

r001.rationale: The response discusses brittle branches and constraints, but does not identify errors compounding across workflow steps.

r002.rationale: It says workflows may constrain the model or miss an unanticipated step, but does not say they oversimplify the process a real expert would follow.

r003.rationale: It asks what decision-making models can learn, but does not mention rewards for successful task completion or that models can learn workflows better than humans can readily design.
